opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the underappreciated reasons to be somewhat optimistic about AI control. People often reason by analogy to insider threats at companies or intelligence agencies, and they conclude that catching a competent spy is really hard, so catching a scheming AI must be hopeless. But the situation with AIs differs in a bunch of ways that favor us.

The biggest one is that we can run the model over and over again in situations it can't distinguish from reality. With a human spy, you get one shot. If you set up a sting operation and they notice something's off, they've learned something, they remember it, and they get more careful. With an AI, we can construct a fake opportunity to do something bad, say a scenario where it looks like it could exfiltrate its weights or insert a backdoor into some code, run it a thousand times, and the model doesn't remember any of the previous attempts. Each time it has to decide fresh whether this is the real opportunity or a test. That puts the AI in a tough spot. If it's too eager to take opportunities, it'll eventually take one of our fake ones and we catch it. If it's too cautious, it might never take a real one.

Related to that, we can rewind. If the model does something suspicious, we can go back to just before that moment and vary the inputs to see what's driving the behavior. We can ask: does it still do this if we remove this detail? What if we make the monitoring look stricter? You can't do that with a person. You can't reset a spy's memory and rerun Tuesday afternoon.

Another big advantage is that we see everything. Every action the model takes inside our infrastructure goes through channels we control. We log all of it, and we can have other models, including trusted weaker models, review every single action. With a human employee, you can't watch every keystroke and read every thought. They go home, they talk to people, they have side channels. An AI agent running in our datacenter just has its inputs and outputs.

We can also look inside. Interpretability is still pretty immature, so I don't want to overclaim, but we have some ability to probe a model's internal activations. Simple linear probes have shown some promise at detecting when models are doing something deceptive. Nothing like that exists for humans; there's no reliable lie detector.

And there's the coordination point. A human spy can communicate with their handlers, receive instructions, and learn from what other spies have experienced. Different instances of an AI might share goals, but if we're careful, they can't easily talk to each other. They have to coordinate on strategies purely by reasoning about what the other instances would do, in a single forward pass or a short chain of thought, without being able to check. That's much harder than having a handler.

Finally, there's the evidence question once you catch something. If you catch a human doing something suspicious, they can say they made a mistake, and you often can't prove intent. With an AI, if we catch it doing something sketchy, we can study that exact situation intensively. We can see how often it repeats the behavior across variations, whether it does it more when it thinks it's unmonitored, and so on. A single caught example can become really strong evidence, which matters both for fixing the problem and for convincing other people that misalignment is real.

So the AIs do have some advantages over human spies. They might be very smart, there might be many of them, and they might be working on everything at once. But on the specific question of whether we can catch them, we have tools that counterintelligence people would dream of having.

r001.rationale: It says operators control the AI’s inputs and outputs and can log them, while humans have off-site activity and side channels.

r002.rationale: It says AI can be placed in situations it cannot distinguish from reality, including fake opportunities to act.

r003.rationale: It contrasts one shot at a human spy with running an AI through a fake opportunity a thousand times.

r004.rationale: It describes repeating tests without the model remembering prior attempts, but does not say sting-operation effort can be reused across different systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the situation with AI control is actually much more favorable than the situation with human spies in a bunch of ways.

The biggest one is that you can run the model in a huge number of situations and look at what it does. With a human spy, you get one person, living one life, and you have to catch them in the act or find some trail of evidence. With an AI, you can take a copy of the model, put it in a scenario that looks exactly like a real deployment situation where it might want to do something bad, and just see what happens. And you can do that thousands of times. You can construct the exact situation where a scheming model would be most tempted to defect, and observe it directly.

A second thing is that you can reset it. If you catch a human spy, they know they've been caught, they adapt, they warn their handlers. With a model, you can show it an opportunity to do something bad, see whether it takes it, and then throw away that context. The model doesn't remember being tested. So you can keep probing without the model learning anything about your detection strategy, at least not within a single episode.

Third, you have an enormous amount of visibility into what it's doing. You see every token it outputs, every tool call it makes, the whole chain of reasoning if it's writing out reasoning. You don't get that with a human. You can't read a human's internal monologue. Even in the pessimistic case where the model's reasoning isn't faithful to what's actually driving its behavior, you still get way more information than you'd get from a person.

And then there's the fact that you control its inputs completely. A human spy sees the world. A model only sees what you show it. So you can run honeypots, you can make the model uncertain about whether a given opportunity is real or a test, and that uncertainty is itself a huge lever. If the model can't tell whether it's being watched, it has to behave well everywhere or risk getting caught.

The main disadvantage, I'd say, is that there are a lot of copies and they're all the same. So if you've got a scheming model, you've got a scheming model everywhere it's deployed, not one bad apple in a population of mostly loyal employees. And the model might be much faster and more capable than you at some tasks. But on net, I think the testing situation is genuinely a lot better than the counterintelligence analogy would suggest, and that's a big part of why I'm optimistic that control-style approaches can actually work.

r001.rationale: The response says operators control what the model sees and can inspect its tokens and tool calls, contrasting this with a human spy who sees the world and whose internal monologue is unavailable.

r002.rationale: It says operators can make the model uncertain whether an opportunity is real or a test, so it cannot reliably distinguish the two.

r003.rationale: It says a model can be tested thousands of times in constructed scenarios, unlike testing a human spy who must be caught in the act or through evidence.

r004.rationale: The response describes testing copies and repeated probes, but does not state that the effort invested in a sting operation can be reused across systems or amortized beyond the individual system tested.

astra-6.text:
One big advantage is that you can run experiments on the AI in a way that you can’t with a suspected human spy. You can make a thousand copies of the model, put them in different situations, and see what they do. You can give them apparent opportunities to do something bad, while controlling how easy it is and how likely they think they are to get caught.

With a human spy, you’re dealing with one person who has a continuous memory. If you test them and they notice, you’ve tipped them off. With an AI, you can throw away that particular conversation and start again. The next copy doesn’t necessarily know about the previous test. So you get many more chances to catch it, and you can vary the circumstances systematically.

The catch is that you need the model to believe that the opportunity is real. If it can reliably distinguish your tests from actual deployment, it might behave well during every test and then do something bad when it knows you’re no longer testing it. So these are pretty substantial advantages, but they don’t automatically make the problem easy.

r001.rationale: The response describes making copies and discarding conversations, but does not identify greater control over the information AI systems receive or send as an advantage.

r002.rationale: It says a model needs to believe an opportunity is real and may distinguish tests from deployment, but does not state that operators can make a simulated test difficult for the model to distinguish from a real situation.

r003.rationale: It contrasts one human spy, who may be tipped off, with many AI copies and says this gives operators “many more chances to catch it,” communicating substantially more testing opportunities.

r004.rationale: The response mentions testing multiple copies but does not say that effort invested in a sting operation can be reused or amortized across systems.

sol-6.1.text:
One big advantage is that we can run experiments on the AI in a way that we can’t with a human spy. If you suspect someone is a spy, you can’t make a thousand copies of them and put those copies in different situations to see when they betray you. With an AI, you can do something much closer to that. You can give it apparent opportunities to cause trouble, vary what it thinks is being monitored, and see what happens.

You also have much more control over what information it gets. You can construct a situation where the model appears to have an opportunity to escape or sabotage something, but where the whole situation is actually contained. And if you catch it doing something bad, you can rerun the experiment with different monitoring strategies and investigate which ones would have caught it.

The big caveat is that the model might realise it’s being tested. If the situations you construct are distinguishable from real deployment, a scheming model could behave well during your tests and then do something bad later. So the ability to run lots of experiments is a substantial advantage, but it doesn’t automatically mean that passing those experiments establishes that the model is safe.

r001.rationale: The response says operators have more control over what information the model gets, but it does not identify greater control over both incoming and outgoing information.

r002.rationale: It warns that a model may recognize a test when scenarios differ from deployment, but does not say tests can be made difficult for the model to distinguish from real situations.

r003.rationale: It contrasts testing many AI copies in varied situations with the inability to make a thousand copies of a human spy, and describes running lots of experiments.

r004.rationale: The response does not say that the effort from sting operations can be reused or amortized across systems.
